conclusion.justification: The report explicitly answers 'no' to the claim, concluding that the best available synthesized evidence does not support that saw palmetto improves urinary symptoms of benign prostatic enlargement more than placebo over longer follow-up. Therefore, it rejects the claim.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion: no.** The best available synthesized evidence does **not** support that saw palmetto (*Serenoa repens*) alone improves urinary symptoms of benign prostatic enlargement/BPH more than placebo over longer follow-up.

An updated systematic review concluded that saw palmetto alone provides “little to no” benefit for men with lower-urinary-tract symptoms due to benign prostatic enlargement; it also noted greater uncertainty for products combined with other herbal agents. This is more persuasive than individual small trials because it systematically evaluates the total randomized-trial evidence.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37345871/

A related systematic review similarly concluded that saw palmetto alone may yield **no clinical benefit** for these symptoms.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34488251/

The evidence includes 12-month randomized trials—an appropriate “longer-term” timeframe for symptom treatment. A PubMed review notes that two trials meeting WHO BPH-consensus criteria (randomized against placebo/standard therapy and lasting 12 months) were published in 2006, including an industry-independent placebo-controlled saw-palmetto trial.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18090484/

This does not mean every person will notice no change—symptoms can fluctuate and placebo responses occur—but average improvement attributable to saw palmetto versus placebo has not been demonstrated. Results for a specific proprietary extract or multi-ingredient product should not automatically be generalized to saw palmetto alone.
